blocks.x: The more you know about an author, the better you understand his writings. Before you start to study Galatians, let's look at the person who wrote this epistle—the great apostle Paul. The more you know about his personal characteristics and experiences, the more clearly you will see why he wrote what he did. Throughout Galatians, we will see Paul defending the Christian faith against the Judaizers. You have already read about the importance of this epistle. Now let's see how God prepared Paul through education and experience to write it.
A. Defender of the Jewish Faith

1) Who were the Galatians? 2) What was the crisis? 3) What was Paul's responsibility? Answering these questions will help you to see more easily the purpose and structure of the book of Galatians.

The southern area was already evangelized at the close of the first missionary journey. It seems that Paul wrote this letter shortly after his first missionary journey and just before his journey to the Jerusalem
Council in A.D. 49. We know that the subjects Paul wrote about in

Galatians were dealt with in the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). If this had taken place already, Paul would surely have mentioned the decisions of the council in Galatians. The council definitely decided that Gentile
Christians would not have to be circumcised or keep the Jewish laws.
Since Paul does not mention this ruling, we may suppose that Galatians was written before the Jerusalem Council.
2. The Crisis in Galatia produced in the churches of Galatia.
The Galatian churches were made up of both Jews and Gentiles. Some

Jewish Christians had always thought that any Gentile who wanted to be saved had to become a Jew and keep the Mosaic Law. But Paul had taught them that Jesus had died for their sins and faith in him brought salvation to Jew and Gentile alike.

Now some questions had arisen that were of vital importance to the Galatians and to Christianity: Is the gospel the Jewish religion plus faith in Jesus Christ? Is Christianity a sect within Judaism, an extension of the Mosaic Law? Does a person need to become a Jew and conform to
Jewish culture in order to be a Christian? Is Christianity a legal system?

Law + Faith = Gospel?

a) Reformers in the Jewish religion.

The basic error of the Judaizers was not that they substituted something for Christ's work, but rather that they tried to add something to it. Have you ever seen anything like that happen? They were distorting the gospel message that Paul had originally given the churches. They insisted that in order to become a good Christian, a person first had to become a good

Jew. They insisted that the Gentile Christians had to be circumcised and keep certain parts of the Jewish law in order to be saved. They taught that salvation is by faith in Christ and by keeping the law.
Do you think that Judaizers were saved? Why or why not?
Describe briefly the crisis of the Gentile Christians in Galatia.
3. Paul’s Responsibility ministers to teach the pure gospel of Jesus Christ and defend the church against error.
What does Paul call the Galatians in 4:19?

You may have noticed when reading Galatians that Paul feels a deep sense of responsibility for these churches. This is because he founded the churches. He won these people to the Lord and loved them like his own children. They were about to turn away from their faith in Christ. Paul— their spiritual father—loved them so much that he wanted to protect them against this danger and strengthen their faith in Christ.
Are you concerned for the spiritual danger that threatens some
person or congregation because of false doctrine? What can you do about it? State the problem as a prayer reminder for yourself and pray about it now.
B. Defense of the Faith Needed in Early Church

To appreciate the importance of the epistle to the Galatians, we must realize that all Christianity faced the same crisis. It was a time of transition. We need to trace briefly some of the events that led to this crisis.
As you move through this second section of Lesson 2 you will look for answers to the following key questions:

1. Transitional Issues in Christianity

At the time of Paul's conversion, the church was made up almost entirely of Jews who had accepted Jesus as their Messiah. There were few Gentile converts. After the mission of Barnabas and Paul, the church began to grow rapidly among the Gentiles. This brought up an important question:

How were these Gentiles to be received into the church? The Judaizers answered, “They must be circumcised and become good Jews as well as have faith in Jesus.” They interpreted Christianity as the Jewish religion plus faith in Jesus Christ. To them, the gospel was an extension of the law of Moses.

C. Defense of the Faith Needed in Today
1. Dealing with Legalism Today churches face today.

Through the ages, Christianity has been threatened and shaken by false doctrine that has crept into the church. Sometimes it has been a legalistic attitude rather than a return to the Torah or law of Moses. Different churches have had their own set of regulations that were considered essential for people to keep if they wanted to go to heaven. Many people still are trusting in their own efforts to lead a Christian life as a way to salvation. Some feel that the social gospel—helping those who are in need—is the path to salvation. Others think that belonging to a Christian church will save them. For all of these Galatians brings God's message for their own spiritual crisis—“The righteous shall live by faith!”

Paul's missionary call came from God, not from people. God had chosen him for his work. God appointed him to preach the gospel to the Gentiles.

Paul had once been an apostle of Judaism sent by the high priest and the Jewish elders to arrest the Christians in Damascus. But on the way he met and surrendered to a higher Authority. The principle in verses 8-9 deals with two truths: 1) The finality of the gospel, 2) The relationship of the messenger to his message.
a. Finality of the Gospel

First, the gospel is a final revelation. There will be no more revelations that will add to the message of God's redeeming work. It is not to be changed or replaced by any newer revelation. The gospel of the grace of

Christ that God sent Paul out to preach—the good news of salvation by faith in Christ—is the true and everlasting gospel. There can be no true revelation of a new way to get right with God, because faith in Christ is the only way.
b. Relationship of Messenger to Message

Second, the gospel becomes the basis for evaluating not only the message but also the messenger. No matter what credentials the messenger may have, these do not commend the message, but rather the message commends the messenger.

b) Accept anything as from the Holy Spirit if a member in good
standing in the church or a minister in good standing gives it as a prophecy, interpretation, or revelation.
c) Judge the source of the message by the kind of life that the
messenger lives.
d) Ask ourselves: “Does the message or revelation agree with
the gospel of Christ?”
